The phenomenological approach to visual arts education—a method that emphasizes direct, lived experience—reconceptualizes the relationship between perceiver and perceived. It establishes a *chiasmic intertwining* (a reciprocal crossing or mutual entanglement of subject and object) that constitutes a pre-reflective stratum of meaning-making. In other words, understanding occurs at a foundational level before conscious analysis takes place.

This ontological reframing (a fundamental shift in how we understand what exists and how we know it) proves particularly generative when applied to post-conceptualist frameworks—artistic approaches that move beyond purely intellectual or concept-based art. This means understanding happens through the body and senses, preceding and informing discursive thought (rational, language-based reasoning).

The hermeneutic implications (interpretive consequences and meanings) of such intersubjective encounters (shared experiences between two or more people) necessitate a reconceptualization of aesthetic experience as fundamentally dialogical—that is, as an ongoing conversation or exchange rather than a one-directional transmission of meaning.

The phenomenological approach to visual arts education offers a new way of understanding the relationship between the viewer and the artwork. Rather than treating these as separate entities, this approach establishes what philosophers call a **chiasmic intertwining**—a mutual crossing-over where viewer and artwork continuously shape one another. This creates a **pre-reflective stratum** (a foundational layer of understanding that exists before conscious analysis) where meaning emerges naturally and intuitively.
